title: Why Teeth Chatter: Shivering Makes 5x the Heat 🥶
description:
Why do your teeth chatter when you're cold? Your brain's hypothalamus makes your muscles shiver to generate heat, and your small, light, hinged jaw rattles so your teeth click together.

Sources:

topic: Why do your teeth chatter when you're cold?
script: Your chattering teeth mean your brain is burning fuel before you freeze. When your skin senses cold, a spot deep in your brain called the hypothalamus hits the panic button. It can't just crank up a thermostat, so it makes your muscles shiver. Tiny fast squeezes, over and over, and every squeeze burns fuel and leaks heat. At full blast, shivering can make about five times the heat your body makes at rest. Your jaw muscles join in too. But your jaw is small and light, and it hangs on a hinge, so every twitch swings it. Top teeth smack bottom teeth. Click, click, click. Your legs and back are shivering too, they're just too heavy to rattle. And honestly, that's kind of genius. Your body turns its own muscles into a furnace. So be honest. When you're freezing, what chatters first, your teeth or your knees?
key_facts: Shivering is involuntary rapid muscle contraction triggered by the brain (hypothalamus) to make heat (PopSci)
Peak shivering measured at 4.9x resting metabolism; ~5x reported (Eur J Appl Physiol 2001, PubMed 11394237)
Chattering happens because face and jaw muscles shiver too, banging the teeth together (ScienceABC)
Jaw is a light, hinged bone, so its shivering is visible/audible while bigger muscles' shivering isn't (explanatory)
